--- title: "Generalized Linear Models (GLMs)" subtitle: "BMLR Chapter 5" format: revealjs: output-file: "05_glm_ch5.html" slide-number: true html: output-file: "05_glm_ch5_o.html" logo: "/img/favicon.png" --- ::: {.cell} ::: ## Learning goals - Explain the use of generalized linear models - Identify the components common to all generalized linear models - Find the canonical link based on the distribution of the response variable # General Linear Models (GLMs) ## Why are GLMs useful? {.smaller} - Linear regression models are used to predict $\mu_{y|x}$. - We assume that $Y$ has a normal distribution with mean $\mu_{y|x}$ and variance $\sigma^2$. - The model we use is $\mu_{y|x}=\beta_0 + \beta_1~x_1 + \beta_2~x_2 +...$ - Note the unknown parameter is on the left and a linear combination of the predictor variables is on the right. - What if the response variable $Y$ doesn't have a normal distribution? Can we estimate a relevant parameter of its actual distribution? - If a GLM exists, then it gives us a way of estimating the relevant parameter using a linear combination of the predictor variables. ## Many models; one family {.smaller} We will see three different situations where glms are appropriate: - linear regression (response has a Normal distribution) - logistic regression (response has a Bernoulli or Binomial distribution) - poisson regression (response has a Poisson or Negative Binomial distribution) . . . All of these cases lead to models that are examples of **generalized linear models**. GLMs have a similar structure for their likelihoods, MLEs, and variances, so we can use a generalized approach to find the model estimates and associated uncertainty. ## Components of a GLM {.smaller} [Nelder and Wdderburn (1972)](https://sakai.duke.edu/access/content/group/ec265469-bdb3-47a7-beb0-317956b6f86f/GLM-paper.pdf) define a broad class of models called **generalized linear models** that generalizes multiple linear regression. GLMs are characterized by three components: . . . 1️⃣ The response variable has a probability function with parameter $\theta$ that can be written in exponential family form (**random component**) . . . 2️⃣ There exists a linear combination of predictors, $\eta = \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p$ (**systematic component**) so that: . . . 3️⃣ A **link** function $g(\theta)$ exists that connects $\theta$ to $\eta$ ::: aside Nelder, J. A., & Wedderburn, R. W. (1972). Generalized linear models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A (General), 135(3), 370-384. ::: ## Math identities that are needed - $a=e^{\log(a)}$ - $a^x = e ^ {x\log(a)}$ - $\log(ab)= \log(a) + \log(b)$ - $\log\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) = \log(a)-\log(b)$ ## Exponential family form {.smaller} Suppose a probability (mass or density) function has a parameter $\theta$. It is said to have a **one-parameter exponential family form** if . . . ✅ The support (set of possible values) does not depend on $\theta$, and . . . ✅ The probability function can be written in the following form $f(y;\theta) = e^{[a(y)b(\theta) + c(\theta) + d(y)]}$ . . . Using this form: $$E(Y) = -\frac{c'(\theta)}{b'(\theta)} \hspace{20mm} Var(Y) = \frac{b''(\theta)c'(\theta) - c''(\theta)b'(\theta)}{[b'(\theta)]^3}$$ . . . Note these last two equations use calculus, so we will not use them. ## Poisson in exponential family form {.smaller} What if our response variable has a Poisson distribution? Can we write the distribution funciton in exponential family form? $$P(Y = y) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!} \hspace{10mm} y = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, \infty$$ . . . $$\begin{aligned}P(Y = y) &= e^{-\lambda}e^{y\log(\lambda)}e^{-\log(y!)}\\ & = e^{y\log(\lambda) - \lambda - \log(y!)}\end{aligned}$$ . . . Recall the form: $f(y;\theta) = e^{[a(y)b(\theta) + c(\theta) + d(y)]}$, where the parameter $\theta = \lambda$ for the Poisson distribution :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - $a(y) = y$ - $b(\lambda) = \log(\lambda)$ ::: :::{.column} - $c(\lambda) = -\lambda$ - $d(y) = -\log(y!)$ ::: :::: ## Poisson in exponential family form {.smaller} - The support for the Poisson distribution is $y = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, \infty$. This does not depend on the parameter $\lambda$. - The probability mass function can be written in the form $f(y;\theta) = e^{[a(y)b(\theta) + c(\theta) + d(y)]}$ . . . **The Poisson distribution can be written in one-parameter exponential family form.** ## Canonical link {.smaller} Suppose there is a response variable $Y$ from a distribution with parameter $\theta$ and a set of predictors that can be written as a linear combination $\eta = \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_j = \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p$
**(There does not have to be an intercept but generally we also include $\beta_0$)**
. . . A **link function**, $g()$, is a monotonic and differentiable function that connects $\theta$ to $\eta$ . . . The **canonical link** is a link function such that $g(\theta) = \eta$ - When working with a member of the one-parameter exponential family, the canonical link is $b(\theta)$ ## Canonical link for Poisson {.smaller} Recall $$P(Y = y) = e^{y\log(\lambda) - \lambda - \log(y!)}$$ then the canonical link is $b(\lambda) = \log(\lambda)$ ## GLM framework: Poisson response variable {.smaller} 1️⃣ Response variable with parameter $\theta$ whose probability function can be written in exponential family form $$P(Y = y) = e^{y\log(\lambda) - \lambda - \log(y!)}$$ . . . 2️⃣ A linear combination of predictors, $\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p$ . . . 3️⃣ A function $g(\lambda)$ that connects $\lambda$ and $\eta$ $$\log(\lambda) = \eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p$$ This means that our linear model will estimate $\log(\lambda)$ rather than just $\lambda$. ## Activity: Identifying canonical link {.smaller} For the distribution - Describe an example of a setting where this random variable may be used. - Identify the parameter. - Write the pmf or pdf in one-parameter exponential form. - Identify the canonical link function - One person from each group: Write your response on the board. ## Activity {.smaller} **Distributions** 1. Binary 2. Exponential 3. Negative binomial (with fixed $r$) 4. Geometric 5. Normal (with fixed $\sigma$) - If your group finishes early, try identifying the canonical link for the other distributions. - See [BMLR - Section 3.6](https://bookdown.org/roback/bookdown-BeyondMLR/ch-distthry.html#additional-resources) for details on the distributions. ## Acknowledgements {.smaller} - These slides are based on content in [BMLR: Chapter 4](https://bookdown.org/roback/bookdown-BeyondMLR/) - Initial versions of the slides are by Dr. Maria Tackett, Duke University - [BMLR: Chapter 5 - Generalized Linear Models: A Unifying Theory](https://bookdown.org/roback/bookdown-BeyondMLR/ch-glms.html) - Nelder, J. A., & Wedderburn, R. W. (1972). Generalized linear models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A (General), 135(3), 370-384. - Generalized Linear Models with Examples in R - Chapter 5 - Generalized Linear Models: Structure - Chapter 6 - Generalized Linear Models: Estimation

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
